sections.html:
Bedford County lies in Virginia's Piedmont, reaching toward the Blue Ridge, with the town of Bedford as its seat. It spans 769 square miles and had 79,462 residents in 2020. Lynchburg, an independent city, sits on its edge, and many newer homes here serve people who commute to Lynchburg or Roanoke or who live near Smith Mountain Lake.

Bedford was an independent city from 1968 and went back to town status, rejoining the county on July 1, 2013. An older deed or letter that names the city is a reason to ask which office carries your parcel today. A few unincorporated areas also use town of Bedford or Lynchburg mailing addresses, so find the county name on your bill and ignore the envelope.

Bedford collects real estate tax in halves: June 5 for the first and December 5 for the second. Billing changed in 2026. Until then a single spring bill carried two coupons, and now each half arrives as its own bill, one in spring and one in fall.

InstallmentDue dateBill
First paymentJune 5Spring bill
Second paymentDecember 5Fall bill
Whole year at onceWith the spring billNo fall bill follows

Settling the full year with the spring bill spares you a second trip. If you are heading toward a sale, ask the treasurer which bills show as paid, since the closing agent will want to know.

• Online, using a bank draft or a credit card.
  • Through the mail.
  • Dropped in the county drop box.
  • At the county office, 122 East Main Street, Bedford, VA 24523.

Your bill shows the tax rate. For the penalty and interest Bedford charges on a late payment, call 540-586-7601, and do it before a deadline passes instead of after. Keep a note of the date and the name of whoever you speak with, so you can point to it if a question comes up later.

Owners who live out of the area can lean on the online or mail options and never visit the office. If a bill is sent to an old address, tell the county in writing so the fall bill does not miss you.

Every parcel in the county is being reassessed, and the new values take effect January 1, 2027. The county contracted Wingate Appraisal Service, which the Virginia Department of Taxation has approved, to move assessed values to current market value. Virginia law requires localities to do this periodically.

Appraisal staff walk neighborhoods and view the exterior of each property. They may take photos for internal use only, and they leave a flyer when nobody is home. Their vehicles are marked Real Estate Assessment/Wingate Appraisal Service, and staff wear ID badges. Owners get reassessment notices ahead of the January 1, 2027 effective date. Questions go to the Reassessment Office at 540-587-0745.

A dispute over your new value goes to the local Board of Equalization. The Reassessment Office can tell you the filing dates and the process that apply to your notice, so call early.

The board must consider and rule on each petition under Virginia Code section 58.1-3381. Its choices are to raise a value, lower it or keep it, and an owner gets notice before any increase. Virginia Cooperative Extension describes the board stage as lasting one to three months.

If the board does not settle things, section 58.1-3984 allows an application to circuit court. The deadline is the later of three years after the tax year ends or one year after the assessment date, among other cases. Judges begin by assuming the assessor is right, so the owner carries the job of proving otherwise by a preponderance of the evidence.

sections.h2: Should you sell before or after January 2027?
sections.html:
Your notice holds the answer. If the new value is higher, the bill after January 1, 2027 grows, and if it is lower, the bill shrinks. Set the notice beside the price you think a buyer will pay.

  • Open the notice the day it arrives and write down the appeal window.
  • If the value looks wrong, ask the Reassessment Office how a review is requested.
  • Before closing, ask the treasurer what you owe for the current year.

A sale before the new values apply lets you settle on the old numbers. A sale after means the buyer carries the new bill from day one, and that can shape what buyers offer.

Tax debt follows the house, not the person. Under Virginia Code section 58.1-3340, the locality holds a lien that outranks the rest until the tax is paid, so sale money goes to the tax first. The contract prorates the current year between you and the buyer.

Late charges have a state ceiling in section 58.1-3916: a penalty no larger than 10 percent of what is overdue (or $10 if higher) and interest no higher than 10 percent a year. Ask the treasurer what Bedford actually applies.

Deed costs are separate. Section 58.1-802 sets a grantor tax of fifty cents on each $500, charged to the seller unless both parties agree otherwise, and section 58.1-801 adds a state recordation tax of 25 cents per $100.

sections.h2: Getting ready for the reassessment notice
sections.html:
Nothing needs to be filed before the notice arrives, but a little preparation pays off. Walk through the house and write down anything an appraiser standing outside could not see: a worn roof, a dated kitchen, a damp basement. Those details matter if you later argue that the value is too high.

Gather recent sales of similar houses near yours, with addresses and dates, and keep them with your notice. If the county flyer turns up on your door, keep it. It shows when staff visited and gives a number to call. When the notice comes, compare the property description line by line with the house. Wrong square footage or a missing outbuilding note is a factual error, and those are the easiest changes to win.

Owners who plan to list in 2027 should also ask a real estate agent how the new value compares with likely sale prices. A value that lands above what buyers will pay is worth a review request, and one that lands below may help a listing. Either way, you will go into the conversation with real numbers in hand and a clear sense of what you want to ask the county.

sections.h2: Who sells to a cash buyer in Bedford County?
sections.html:
Heirs, landlords with a house that needs work and owners who live far away are the people who most often choose cash. A reassessment, two separate tax bills and a list of repairs can each tip the decision.

We purchase houses as they stand. Send the Bedford County address by phone or text, and a written cash offer will follow.

faqs.q: When are Bedford County property taxes due?
faqs.a: June 5 and December 5. Starting in 2026, owners receive two separate bills, one in the spring and one in the fall.

faqs.q: When does the Bedford County reassessment take effect?
faqs.a: January 1, 2027. Notices go out ahead of that date.

faqs.q: Who is doing the Bedford County reassessment?
faqs.a: Wingate Appraisal Service, hired by the county and approved by the Virginia Department of Taxation. Call 540-587-0745 with questions.

faqs.q: Is the town of Bedford separate from Bedford County?
faqs.a: Bedford was an independent city from 1968 and reverted to a town, then rejoined the county on July 1, 2013. It is the county seat.

faqs.q: How can I pay my Bedford County real estate tax?
faqs.a: Online by bank draft or credit card, by mail, in the drop box or in person at 122 East Main Street, Bedford.
